title: SPC severe weather watch probabilities did not scale with watch area and duration in 12,924 US watches (2006-2025, report-based truth), and a size-duration correction improved 2026 forecasts
abstract: We did a pre-registered reliability test of the NOAA Storm Prediction Center (SPC) watch probability tables (WWP). Each tornado or severe thunderstorm watch gives seven probabilities, for example 2 or more tornadoes or 10 or more severe hail reports in the watch. We matched 12,924 watches from 2006-2025 to the final SPC severe report database, with the SPC county list of each watch and its issue-to-expiry time. Two elements had a large mean bias: 1 or more wind report of 65 kt or more occurred 1.44 times as often as stated (95% CI 1.40-1.48, Brier skill 0.00), and 10 or more hail reports 0.72 times (0.69-0.74). Other elements had O/E 0.83-1.04. The main error was conditional. Per tenfold watch area, the log-odds of the observed frequency rose by 1.7-2.8, but the log-odds of the stated probability rose by only 0.3-1.5. The stated probabilities did not rise with watch duration, but observed log-odds rose by 1.0-3.8 per tenfold duration. Small watches (median 42,000 km2) had O/E 0.36-0.80 for six elements; large watches (128,000 km2) 0.97-1.80. The result was the same with three other area and time definitions. Models fitted on 2006-2025 with area and duration added increased the ROC area for all six testable elements on 699 watches in 2026 (preliminary reports), for example from 0.70 to 0.79 for 65 kt wind. Wind-report counts depended on population density (pre-registered). Exploratory checks link the hail bias to the 2010 change of the severe hail size and to fewer hail reports after 2018, and the 65 kt wind bias to lower stated probabilities in 2013-2017 and more measured gusts. Truth is storm reports, which are incomplete and depend on population; the 2026 test uses preliminary reports that under-count 65 kt wind and hail.
